know: Three modes: conduction (Fourier), convection (Newton's law of cooling), radiation (Stefan–Boltzmann). A surface often loses heat by two or three at once.
Heat rate $q$ in W; heat flux $q''=q/A$ in W/m². The sign tells direction, so draw the arrow first.
Radiation temperatures must be absolute (K). For a small surface in large surroundings use $\varepsilon\sigma(T_s^4-T_{sur}^4)$, or the linearized $h_r$.
Energy balance on a control volume: $\dot E_{in}-\dot E_{out}+\dot E_g=\dot E_{st}$. At a surface there is no volume, so conduction in = convection out + radiation out.
Steady state means $\dot E_{st}=0$. Always state your assumptions (steady, 1-D, constant properties).

eq.label: Energy balance
eq.tex: \dot E_{in}-\dot E_{out}+\dot E_g=\dot E_{st}=\rho c_p V\,\frac{dT}{dt}

pitfalls: Using °C in the radiation term.
Forgetting radiation when $h$ is a natural-convection value (radiation is often equal in size).
Mixing up $q$ (W), $q'$ (W/m) and $q''$ (W/m²).

recall.q: A hot surface sits in room air. Name every way heat leaves it and write the equation for each.
recall.a: Convection $q''=h(T_s-T_\infty)$ and radiation $q''=\varepsilon\sigma(T_s^4-T_{sur}^4)$ leave the surface; conduction (Fourier, $q''=-k\,dT/dx$) brings heat to it. At a surface there is no volume, so conduction in = convection out + radiation out.

recall.q: Write the control-volume energy balance. What drops out at steady state?
recall.a: $\dot E_{in}-\dot E_{out}+\dot E_g=\dot E_{st}$. Steady state means $\dot E_{st}=0$. State the assumptions you used (steady, 1-D, constant properties).

recall.q: What does $h_r$ do for you, and which temperatures go into it?
recall.a: It linearizes radiation: $q''_{rad}=h_r(T_s-T_{sur})$ with $h_r=\varepsilon\sigma(T_s+T_{sur})(T_s^2+T_{sur}^2)$. All temperatures in kelvin.

problems.title: Hot plate: convection plus radiation
problems.statement: A thin flat plate of area $A=0.5\ \mathrm{m^2}$ has one face at $T_s=90^\circ$C, exposed to room air at $T_\infty=25^\circ$C with $h=18\ \mathrm{W/m^2K}$ and to large surroundings at $T_{sur}=25^\circ$C. The surface emissivity is $\varepsilon=0.8$. (a) Find the convective and radiative heat fluxes. (b) Find the radiation heat-transfer coefficient $h_r$ and the total heat rate from the face.
problems.hint: Radiation always needs kelvin. Convection and radiation from the same surface add (parallel paths).

steps: Linearize radiation: $h_r=\varepsilon\sigma(T_s+T_{sur})(T_s^2+T_{sur}^2)=6.62\ \mathrm{W/m^2K}$ — comparable to $h$, so radiation cannot be ignored here.

problems.title: Chip energy balance (find the surface temperature)
problems.statement: A square chip, $20\times20$ mm, dissipates $P=2$ W. Its back and edges are perfectly insulated, so all the power leaves through the top face to $T_\infty=22^\circ$C air ($h=60\ \mathrm{W/m^2K}$) and by radiation to surroundings at 22 °C ($\varepsilon=0.9$). Write the surface energy balance and find the steady surface temperature. How much error results from ignoring radiation?
problems.hint: Setting up the balance on the correct control surface is where the points are.

steps: Control surface at the top face: $E_{in}-E_{out}=0$, so $P/A=q''_{conv}+q''_{rad}$, i.e. $P/A=h(T_s-T_\infty)+\varepsilon\sigma(T_s^4-T_{sur}^4)$. Here $P/A=5000$ W/m².
The equation is quartic in $T_s$, so iterate (or use the linearized $h_r$): guess $T_s$, compute both fluxes, adjust until they sum to $P/A$.
Convection only: $T_s=T_\infty+P/(hA)=105.3^\circ$C. Ignoring radiation overpredicts the surface temperature by about 9 K.

problems.method: Surface energy balance (power in = convection + radiation out)

know: The heat equation is an energy balance on a differential volume. Steady, 1-D, constant $k$, no generation reduces it to $d^2T/dx^2=0$ (plane wall).
Know the three coordinate forms. In cylinders and spheres the area changes, so the $r$ factors stay inside the derivative.
Thermal diffusivity $\alpha=k/\rho c_p$ measures how quickly temperature disturbances spread.
Boundary conditions: fixed temperature, fixed flux (adiabatic is zero flux), convection at a surface. Transient problems also need an initial condition.
A curved temperature profile in steady state means generation or variable $k$.

eq.label: Heat equation (Cartesian)
eq.tex: \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\left(k\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}\right)+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\!\left(k\frac{\partial T}{\partial y}\right)+\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\!\left(k\frac{\partial T}{\partial z}\right)+\dot q=\rho c_p\frac{\partial T}{\partial t}

eq.label: Cylindrical, 1-D radial
eq.tex: \frac1r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\!\left(kr\frac{\partial T}{\partial r}\right)+\dot q=\rho c_p\frac{\partial T}{\partial t}

eq.label: Spherical, 1-D radial
eq.tex: \frac1{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\!\left(kr^2\frac{\partial T}{\partial r}\right)+\dot q=\rho c_p\frac{\partial T}{\partial t}

pitfalls: Taking $r$ outside the derivative in cylindrical/spherical forms.
Writing the convection boundary condition with the wrong sign — draw the heat-flow direction first.
Losing an integration constant: count constants vs. boundary conditions.

recall.q: Write the 1-D, steady, constant-$k$ plane-wall heat equation with no generation, and its general solution.
recall.a: $d^2T/dx^2=0$, so $T=C_1x+C_2$: a straight line. Two boundary conditions fix the two constants.

recall.q: Name three types of boundary condition and write the convection one at $x=0$ with heat flowing in the $+x$ direction.
recall.a: Fixed temperature $T(0)=T_s$; fixed flux $-k\,\partial T/\partial x=q''_s$ (adiabatic: zero flux); convection $-k\,\partial T/\partial x|_{x=0}=h[T_\infty-T(0)]$. Draw the heat-flow arrow first to get the sign.

recall.q: What does a curved steady temperature profile in a plane wall tell you, and what does $\alpha$ measure?
recall.a: Generation or temperature-dependent $k$ (in cylinders and spheres the area change curves it anyway). $\alpha=k/\rho c_p$ measures how fast a temperature disturbance spreads.

problems.title: Reading a temperature profile
problems.statement: Steady one-dimensional conduction occurs in a plane wall of thickness $L=0.10$ m and $k=15\ \mathrm{W/m\,K}$. The measured temperature distribution is $T(x)=120-1000x-20000x^2$ with $T$ in °C and $x$ in m. (a) Find the heat flux at $x=0$ and $x=L$. (b) Use the heat diffusion equation to find the volumetric generation rate $\dot q$. (c) Confirm with an overall energy balance on the wall.
problems.hint: Differentiate once for the flux, twice for $\dot q$. A profile with curvature means generation (or variable k).

steps: Fourier: $q''_x=-k\,dT/dx=-15(-1000-40000x)$. At $x=0$: $q''=15000$ W/m²; at $x=L$: $q''=75000$ W/m² (both positive: flow is in $+x$).
1-D steady heat equation with generation: $k\,d^2T/dx^2+\dot q=0\Rightarrow\dot q=-k(2c)=-15(-40000)=6.00\times10^{5}$ W/m³.

Overall balance (steady): $\dot E_{in}-\dot E_{out}+\dot E_g=0$ per unit area: $q''(0)-q''(L)+\dot qL=15000-75000+60000=0$ ✓. More energy leaves at $x=L$ than enters at $x=0$, exactly the generated amount.

problems.method: Fourier's law applied to a given temperature profile

problems.title: Radial profile in a heated rod
problems.statement: A long solid rod of radius $r_0=20$ mm and $k=20\ \mathrm{W/m\,K}$ has steady radial temperatures $T(r)=T_0-Ar^2$ with $A=5\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{K/m^2}$. (a) Start from the cylindrical heat equation and find $\dot q$. (b) Find the surface heat flux and the heat rate per unit length. (c) Verify with an energy balance. (d) How much hotter is the centerline than the surface?
problems.hint: Use the radial form with the $r$ inside the derivative. Check units of $\dot q$.

steps: Cylindrical, steady, 1-D: $\dfrac1r\dfrac{d}{dr}\!\left(kr\dfrac{dT}{dr}\right)+\dot q=0$. With $dT/dr=-2Ar$: $r\,dT/dr=-2Ar^2$, derivative $=-4Ar$, so $\dot q=4Ak=4.00\times10^{7}$ W/m³.
Surface flux (outward): $q''(r_0)=-k\,dT/dr=2Akr_0=4.00\times10^{5}$ W/m²; per unit length $q'=q''(2\pi r_0)=50265$ W/m.
Energy balance on a unit length: generated $=\dot q\pi r_0^2=50265$ W/m $=q'$ ✓.

know: Plane wall: $q=\Delta T/R_{tot}$ with series resistances $R_{cond}=L/kA$, $R_{conv}=1/hA$, and $R_{rad}=1/h_rA$. Same $q$ through every series element, so $\Delta T_i=qR_i$.
Parallel paths combine like resistors in parallel. Contact resistance $R''_{t,c}$ sits at layer interfaces.
Cylinder (per length): $R'_{cond}=\ln(r_2/r_1)/2\pi k$; sphere: $R=(1/r_1-1/r_2)/4\pi k$. In radial systems $q$ is constant but $q''$ falls with radius.
Critical radius of insulation $r_{cr}=k/h$ (cylinder) or $2k/h$ (sphere): insulating below it increases heat loss.
Overall coefficient: $q=UA\,\Delta T$ with $1/UA=R_{tot}$.
pitfalls: Putting convection resistance on only one side.
Using the wrong area in cylindrical $R$ (the log form already contains it).
Treating $q''$ as constant in a cylinder.

recall.q: Draw the resistance network for a wall with fluid on both sides. Give each resistance and the heat rate.
recall.a: Three in series: $1/h_1A$, $L/kA$, $1/h_2A$. $q=(T_{\infty,1}-T_{\infty,2})/R_{tot}$, and the same $q$ passes through every series element.

recall.q: In a pipe wall, which quantity is constant with radius and which falls? Give the resistance per unit length.
recall.a: $q$ is constant; $q''=q/2\pi rL$ falls with $r$. $R'_{cond}=\ln(r_2/r_1)/2\pi k$.

recall.q: What is the critical radius of insulation for a cylinder and a sphere, and what does it mean?
recall.a: $r_{cr}=k/h$ (cylinder), $2k/h$ (sphere). If the outer radius is below it, adding insulation increases the heat loss.

problems.title: Composite wall with contact resistance
problems.statement: An exterior wall is built, from inside to outside, of gypsum board ($L=12.5$ mm, $k=0.17$), glass-fiber insulation ($L=80$ mm, $k=0.04$) and brick ($L=120$ mm, $k=0.70$; all W/m·K). Imperfect contact between the insulation and brick gives $R''_{t,c}=0.020\ \mathrm{m^2K/W}$. Inside air is $21^\circ$C with $h_i=8\ \mathrm{W/m^2K}$; outside air is $-10^\circ$C with $h_o=25\ \mathrm{W/m^2K}$. Draw the thermal circuit, then find (a) the heat loss per m², (b) the inside wall-surface temperature, and (c) the temperature drop across the contact resistance.
problems.hint: Same $q''$ flows through every series element. $\Delta T=q''R''$ for each.

steps: Contact drop: $\Delta T_c=q''R''_{t,c}=12.76(0.020)=0.255$ K. (Interface temperatures on either side: -7.05 °C and -7.30 °C.)

problems.method: Series thermal circuit with contact resistance

problems.title: Insulated steam pipe and critical radius
problems.statement: A steam pipe of outer radius $r_1=30$ mm has an outer wall at $150^\circ$C. It is wrapped with insulation ($k=0.05\ \mathrm{W/m\,K}$, outer radius $r_2=55$ mm). Surrounding air is $20^\circ$C with a combined (convection+radiation) coefficient $h=15\ \mathrm{W/m^2K}$. (a) Find the heat loss per meter of pipe and the outer insulation-surface temperature. (b) Find the critical radius and say whether this insulation is helping. (c) Compare with the bare pipe.
problems.hint: In cylindrical coordinates the conduction resistance is a log term per unit length.

steps: Radial circuit: $R'_{cond}=\dfrac{\ln(r_2/r_1)}{2\pi k}=1.9294$ m·K/W; $R'_{conv}=\dfrac1{2\pi r_2h}=0.1929$ m·K/W.
Critical radius (cylinder) $r_{cr}=k/h=3.33$ mm $<r_1=30$ mm, so any added insulation reduces the loss.
Bare pipe: $q'=h(2\pi r_1)(T_1-T_\infty)=368$ W/m, so the insulation cuts the loss by 83%.

know: Plane wall with symmetric cooling: $T(x)=T_s+\dfrac{\dot q}{2k}(L^2-x^2)$, maximum at the midplane.
Cylinder: $T(r)=T_s+\dfrac{\dot qr_o^2}{4k}(1-r^2/r_o^2)$; sphere: $\dfrac{\dot qr_o^2}{6k}$.
Surface temperature comes from an overall energy balance: all generated heat leaves through the surface by convection (and radiation).
Use Appendix C's summary instead of re-deriving, but know how the derivation goes (instructor's slides: 3B).
Check: heat leaving $=\dot q\times$ volume.
pitfalls: Using the full thickness instead of half-thickness $L$.
Forgetting the symmetry condition $dT/dx=0$ at the midplane.
Using $\dot q$ (W/m³) where a flux (W/m²) is needed.

recall.q: Write $T(x)$ for a plane wall of thickness $2L$ with uniform generation and symmetric cooling. Where is $T_{max}$?
recall.a: $T(x)=T_s+\dfrac{\dot qL^2}{2k}\left(1-\dfrac{x^2}{L^2}\right)$, maximum at the midplane $x=0$ because $dT/dx=0$ there by symmetry.

recall.q: Where does $T_s$ come from?
recall.a: All the generated heat leaves through the surface: $\dot qL=h(T_s-T_\infty)$, so $T_s=T_\infty+\dot qL/h$ (cylinder $\dot qr_o/2h$, sphere $\dot qr_o/3h$).

recall.q: What is the centerline-to-surface temperature rise for a cylinder and for a sphere?
recall.a: Cylinder $\dot qr_o^2/4k$, sphere $\dot qr_o^2/6k$ (plane wall $\dot qL^2/2k$).

problems.title: Plane wall with generation, convection both sides
problems.statement: A wall of thickness $2L=40$ mm ($k=25$ W/m·K) generates $\dot q=2\times10^6\ \mathrm{W/m^3}$ uniformly. Both surfaces see fluid at $100^\circ$C with $h=1000\ \mathrm{W/m^2K}$. (a) Derive $T(x)$ using the midplane as $x=0$. (b) Find the surface and midplane temperatures. (c) Where is the maximum temperature?
problems.hint: Do the energy balance at the surface instead of fighting the second boundary condition algebraically.

steps: Surface energy balance at $x=L$: heat conducted to the surface equals heat convected away, $\dot qL=h(T_s-T_\infty)$, so $T_s=T_\infty+\dot qL/h=140.0^\circ$C.
Maximum temperature is at the midplane $x=0$ (symmetry, adiabatic there).

problems.title: Current-carrying wire
problems.statement: A long nichrome wire ($D=3$ mm, $k=20$ W/m·K, electrical resistivity $\rho_e=1.08\times10^{-6}\ \Omega\,$m) carries $I=30$ A in $25^\circ$C air with $h=100\ \mathrm{W/m^2K}$. Find (a) $\dot q$, (b) the surface temperature, and (c) the centerline-to-surface temperature difference. Which resistance dominates?
problems.hint: Convert current into $\dot q$ first. Surface energy balance sets $T_s$, conduction only sets the small internal rise.

steps: $A_c=\pi D^2/4=7.07\times10^{-6}$ m²; $R'_e=\rho_e/A_c=0.1528\ \Omega$/m; power per length $q'=I^2R'_e=137.5$ W/m; $\dot q=q'/A_c=1.95\times10^{7}$ W/m³.
Steady: all generated heat leaves by convection: $q'=h\pi D(T_s-T_\infty)$, so $T_s=T_\infty+\dfrac{q'}{\pi Dh}=170.9^\circ$C.
Solid cylinder with generation: $T_0-T_s=\dfrac{\dot qr_o^2}{4k}=0.55$ K.
Convection resistance dominates by a factor of several hundred: the wire is essentially isothermal.

problems.method: Joule heating, then the cylinder-with-generation profile

know: Fin equation $d^2\theta/dx^2-m^2\theta=0$ with $m^2=hP/kA_c$. Tip conditions (Table 3.4): convective tip, adiabatic tip, fixed tip temperature, infinite fin.
Adiabatic tip: $q_f=M\tanh mL$. For a convective tip, use the corrected length $L_c=L+A_c/P$ (that is $L+D/4$ for a pin, $L+t/2$ for a thin rectangular fin) in the adiabatic formula.
Fin efficiency $\eta_f=q_f/q_{max}$ where $q_{max}=hA_f\theta_b$; Table 3.5 gives $\eta_f$ for common shapes.
Arrays: $\eta_o=1-\dfrac{NA_f}{A_t}(1-\eta_f)$ and $q_t=\eta_ohA_t\theta_b$ (or add fin heat rates plus the unfinned base).
Fins help most when $h$ is low (gases) and $k$ is high; fin effectiveness $\varepsilon_f=q_f/(hA_{c,b}\theta_b)$ should be >2 to justify a fin.
pitfalls: Using the wrong perimeter $P$ or cross-section $A_c$.
Forgetting the unfinned base area in an array.
Using the adiabatic-tip result with a short, fat fin without correcting the length.

recall.q: Write the fin equation and the fin parameter $m$.
recall.a: $d^2\theta/dx^2-m^2\theta=0$ with $m=\sqrt{hP/kA_c}$.

recall.q: Give the adiabatic-tip heat rate and the quick way to handle a convective tip.
recall.a: $q_f=M\tanh mL$ with $M=\sqrt{hPkA_c}\,\theta_b$. For a convective tip use the corrected length $L_c=L+A_c/P$ ($L+D/4$ for a pin, $L+t/2$ for a thin fin) in the same formula.

recall.q: Define fin efficiency and effectiveness. When is a fin worth adding?
recall.a: $\eta_f=q_f/(hA_f\theta_b)$; $\varepsilon_f=q_f/(hA_{c,b}\theta_b)$ should exceed about 2. Fins pay off when $h$ is low (gases) and $k$ is high.

problems.title: Pin fin: heat rate and efficiency
problems.statement: An aluminum pin fin ($k=200$ W/m·K) has diameter $D=4$ mm and length $L=40$ mm. Its base is at $120^\circ$C and the air is $25^\circ$C with $h=50\ \mathrm{W/m^2K}$ (also acting on the tip). (a) Find $m$ and $mL$. (b) Find the heat rate with the convective tip, and compare with the adiabatic-tip and corrected-length approximations. (c) Find the fin efficiency.
problems.hint: Corrected length is the fastest accurate shortcut on an exam.

steps: Convective tip: $q_f=M\dfrac{\sinh mL+(h/mk)\cosh mL}{\cosh mL+(h/mk)\sinh mL}$ with $h/mk=0.0158$, giving $q_f=2.154$ W.
Adiabatic tip: $M\tanh mL=2.113$ W (a 1.9% underprediction). Corrected length $L_c=L+D/4=0.0410$ m: $M\tanh mL_c=2.154$ W (within 0.00% of the exact convective-tip value).
Efficiency: $\eta_f=q_f/(hA_f\theta_b)$ with $A_f=\pi DL+\pi D^2/4=5.15\times10^{-4}$ m², so $\eta_f=0.880$.

problems.method: Fin heat rate with corrected length

know: Table 4.1 cases to know: (1) sphere buried in a semi-infinite medium, (2) horizontal cylinder buried in a semi-infinite medium, (3) vertical cylinder, (4) two cylinders in an infinite medium. These are the first four cases the study guide names.
$q=Sk(T_1-T_2)$ where $S$ has units of length. Compose with 1-D shape factors: wall $A/L$, cylinder $2\pi L/\ln(r_2/r_1)$, sphere $4\pi r_1r_2/(r_2-r_1)$.
Two isothermal boundaries only. Resistance form: $R=1/(Sk)$.
Check restrictions ($L\gg D$, $z>D/2$) before using a formula.
pitfalls: Using $z$ where the formula needs $2z/D$.
Applying the formula to a surface that is not isothermal.
Ignoring that $S$ is a length, not an area.
samples: Test 2 guide: §4.3 and Table 4.1, first four cases only

recall.q: Write the heat rate with a shape factor. What are the units of $S$ and the resistance form?
recall.a: $q=Sk(T_1-T_2)$. $S$ is a length (m). $R=1/(Sk)$.

recall.q: Write $S$ for a sphere buried in a semi-infinite medium and the conditions that must hold.
recall.a: $S=\dfrac{2\pi D}{1-D/4z}$ for $z>D/2$, with isothermal sphere and isothermal ground surface.

recall.q: Write $S$ for a horizontal buried cylinder and its log approximation.
recall.a: $S=\dfrac{2\pi L}{\cosh^{-1}(2z/D)}$, approximately $\dfrac{2\pi L}{\ln(4z/D)}$ when $z>3D/2$ and $L\gg D$.

problems.title: Hot sphere in a large soil mass (resistance form)
problems.statement: A spherical heat source of diameter $D=0.50$ m is buried deep in soil of $k=1.5$ W/m·K, far from any surface, so the soil acts as an infinite medium. The sphere surface is at $80^\circ$C and the soil far away is at $20^\circ$C. Find the shape factor, the conduction resistance and the heat rate. What happens to the heat rate if $D$ doubles?
problems.hint: Shape factor $S$ has units of length; resistance is $1/(Sk)$.

steps: Isothermal sphere in an infinite medium (Table 4.1): $S=2\pi D=3.142$ m.
$S\propto D$, so doubling $D$ doubles the heat rate to 565.5 W.

problems.title: Buried pipe (Table 4.1, horizontal cylinder)
problems.statement: A hot-water pipe of diameter $D=0.20$ m and length $L=30$ m is buried with its axis $z=1.5$ m below the ground surface. The pipe wall is at $60^\circ$C, the ground surface is held at $5^\circ$C and the soil has $k=1.0$ W/m·K. Find the shape factor and the heat loss. Compare the exact $\cosh^{-1}$ expression with the $\ln(4z/D)$ approximation.
problems.hint: Use the ratio $2z/D$, not $z/D$, inside the $\cosh^{-1}$ expression.

steps: Two-dimensional conduction between two isothermal boundaries, so $q=Sk(T_1-T_2)$. Table 4.1, horizontal isothermal cylinder in a semi-infinite medium ($L\gg D$): $S=\dfrac{2\pi L}{\cosh^{-1}(2z/D)}$.

problems.title: Buried spherical tank (Table 4.1, sphere)
problems.statement: A spherical tank of diameter $D=2$ m contains a process fluid so that its wall is at $40^\circ$C. The center is $z=4$ m below a ground surface at $10^\circ$C; the soil has $k=1.2$ W/m·K. Find the heat loss. By what percentage would you misestimate it if you treated the soil as an infinite medium?
problems.hint: Both cases-1-through-4 formulas appear in Table 4.1, which the study guide says to know.

steps: Table 4.1, isothermal sphere in a semi-infinite medium ($z>D/2$): $S=\dfrac{2\pi D}{1-D/4z}=\dfrac{12.566}{1-0.125}=14.36$ m.
Infinite medium: $S=2\pi D=12.57$ m, a 12.5% underestimate — the nearby surface (at $10^\circ$C) increases the loss.

know: Write an energy balance on each node's control volume. Interior node with no generation: $T_{m,n}$ is the average of its four neighbors.
Boundary nodes (Table 4.2): plane surface with convection, external corner, internal corner, insulated boundary (mirror image). Each has its own $Bi=h\Delta x/k$ terms.
Solve by matrix inversion or Gauss–Seidel iteration (needs a diagonally dominant system).
Use symmetry to cut unknowns. Check the final answer by an overall energy balance.
pitfalls: Dropping the factor of 2 on the interior neighbor at a convective surface.
Using the plane-surface formula at a corner.
Changing $\Delta x$ or $\Delta y$ without rescaling terms.

recall.q: Write the interior-node equation with and without generation.
recall.a: No generation: $T_{m,n}$ is the average of its four neighbors. With generation: $T_{m,n}=\tfrac14\left(\sum T_{nb}+\dot q\Delta x^2/k\right)$.

recall.q: Write the node equation for a plane surface with convection.
recall.a: $T_{m,n+1}+T_{m,n-1}+2T_{m-1,n}+2Bi\,T_\infty-2(Bi+2)T_{m,n}=0$ with $Bi=h\Delta x/k$. Note the factor 2 on the interior neighbor.

recall.q: Name two ways to cut the work and one check on the answer.
recall.a: Use symmetry (an adiabatic or symmetry line acts as a mirror image) and Gauss–Seidel or a small matrix solve. Check with an overall energy balance.

problems.title: Interior node with generation
problems.statement: An interior node of a square grid ($\Delta x=\Delta y=10$ mm) has neighbors at $80$, $60$, $70$ and $90^\circ$C. The material has $k=20$ W/m·K and generates heat uniformly at $\dot q=5\times10^5\ \mathrm{W/m^3}$. Write the nodal equation and find the node temperature (steady state).
problems.hint: Without generation the node is the average of its neighbors; generation adds $\dot q\Delta x^2/k$ to the sum.

steps: Energy balance on the node's cell: $T_{up}+T_{down}+T_{left}+T_{right}-4T_{m,n}+\dfrac{\dot q\,\Delta x^2}{k}=0$.
Generation term: $\dot q\Delta x^2/k=2.50$ K. Sum of neighbors $=300$.
$T_{m,n}=\dfrac{300+2.50}{4}=75.62^\circ$C (a bit above the plain average of 75.0$^\circ$C because of generation).

problems.title: Four-node finite-difference solution
problems.statement: A square plate has its top edge held at $100^\circ$C and its left, right and bottom edges at $0^\circ$C. The plate is discretized with $\Delta x=\Delta y$ so that there are four interior nodes: nodes 1 (top-left) and 2 (top-right) in the top row, nodes 3 (bottom-left) and 4 (bottom-right) in the bottom row (each one grid spacing from its neighboring edges). Write the finite-difference equation for each node and solve for the temperatures. Use symmetry as a check.
problems.hint: One equation per unknown; exploit symmetry to reduce to 2×2.

steps: Symmetry about the vertical centerline gives $T_1=T_2=a$, $T_3=T_4=b$: $3a-b=100$ and $3b=a$.

problems.title: Convective boundary node
problems.statement: A node lies on a plane surface exposed to fluid at $T_\infty=20^\circ$C with $Bi=h\Delta x/k=0.5$. Its two neighbors along the surface (above and below) are at $90^\circ$C each, and its interior neighbor (one $\Delta x$ into the solid) is at $85^\circ$C. Derive the energy balance for the node and find its temperature. No generation, steady state.
problems.hint: Remember the factor of 2 on the interior neighbor and the $Bi$ term; the corner-node version has different coefficients.

steps: Control volume is a half-cell of size $\Delta x/2\times\Delta y$: conduction in from the interior neighbor (full height) and from the two side neighbors (half height each), plus convection from the fluid.

know: $Bi=hL_c/k$ with $L_c=V/A_s$ (not the radius). If $Bi<0.1$, assume a uniform temperature.
Energy balance with convection only: $\rho Vc\,dT/dt=-hA_s(T-T_\infty)$, solution $\theta/\theta_i=e^{-t/\tau_t}$ with $\tau_t=\rho Vc/hA_s$.
Total energy removed: $Q=\rho Vc\,\theta_i(1-e^{-t/\tau_t})$. After $3\tau_t$ about 5% of the difference remains.
Add radiation, generation or surface flux to the balance when stated (§5.3). These usually give an ODE that is no longer a pure exponential.
pitfalls: Using $L_c=r$ for a sphere (it is $r/3$).
Skipping the $Bi$ check.
Forgetting a face is insulated when computing $A_s$.

recall.q: What is the first step of every transient problem, and the threshold?
recall.a: Compute $Bi=hL_c/k$ with $L_c=V/A_s$. If $Bi<0.1$ the body is lumped (uniform temperature).

recall.q: Write the lumped solution and the time constant. How much is left after three time constants?
recall.a: $\dfrac{T-T_\infty}{T_i-T_\infty}=e^{-t/\tau_t}$, $\tau_t=\rho Vc/hA_s$. After $3\tau_t$ about 5% of the initial difference remains.

recall.q: Give $L_c=V/A_s$ for a sphere, a long cylinder and a cube.
recall.a: Sphere $D/6=r/3$; long cylinder $D/4=r/2$; cube $a/6$. For a plate cooled on both faces it is half the thickness.

problems.title: Which bodies can be treated as lumped?
problems.statement: Three spheres start hot and are cooled by a fluid. (A) copper, $D=10$ mm, $k=401$ W/m·K, $h=50$ W/m²K. (B) stainless steel, $D=50$ mm, $k=15$ W/m·K, $h=500$ W/m²K. (C) glass, $D=20$ mm, $k=1.4$ W/m·K, $h=100$ W/m²K. For each, find the Biot number and decide whether lumped capacitance is valid.
problems.hint: Use $L_c=V/A_s$; for a sphere that is $D/6$.

steps: For a sphere $L_c=V/A_s=D/6$ (not the radius). Then $Bi=hL_c/k$ and compare with 0.1.
Conductive solids with small $h$ are lumped; poor conductors or large $h$ need the spatial (one-term or numerical) methods.

problems.title: Quenching a steel ball (lumped capacitance)
problems.statement: A steel sphere ($\rho=7800$ kg/m³, $c=470$ J/kg·K, $k=44$ W/m·K) of diameter $25$ mm at $500^\circ$C is quenched in an oil bath at $40^\circ$C with $h=300\ \mathrm{W/m^2K}$. (a) Check whether the lumped-capacitance method is valid. (b) Find the time constant and the time to reach $100^\circ$C. (c) How much energy has left the ball by then?
problems.hint: Characteristic length is $V/A_s$, not the radius. Always compute $Bi$ first.

steps: $L_c=V/A_s=D/6=0.00417$ m, $Bi=hL_c/k=0.0284$ < 0.1, so lumped capacitance is valid.

problems.title: Thin plate cooling in air
problems.statement: A thin aluminum plate ($\rho=2700$, $c=900$ J/kg·K, $k=237$ W/m·K), $2$ mm thick, at $200^\circ$C is suddenly exposed on both faces to air at $25^\circ$C with $h=35\ \mathrm{W/m^2K}$ (neglect edges and radiation). (a) Show that the plate is effectively isothermal. (b) Find the time to cool to $60^\circ$C. (c) What happens to that time if $h$ is doubled? (d) What fraction of the initial temperature difference remains after $3\tau_t$?
problems.hint: Two exposed faces: the characteristic length is half the thickness.

steps: Doubling $h$ halves $\tau_t$ and so halves the time: $t=56$ s.
$\theta/\theta_i=e^{-3}=0.050$ — about 5% of the initial difference remains.

know: Dimensionless variables: $\theta^*=\theta/\theta_i$, $x^*=x/L$, $Fo=\alpha t/L^2$, $Bi=hL/k$ with $L$ the half-thickness (wall) or $r_o$ (cylinder, sphere).
One-term series valid for $Fo>0.2$: $\theta^*=C_1e^{-\zeta_1^2Fo}\times$ shape function. Find $\zeta_1,C_1$ from Table 5.1 or solve the eigenvalue equation.
Center temperature first: $\theta_o^*=C_1e^{-\zeta_1^2Fo}$. Then other positions via the cosine / $J_0$ / sine function.
Total energy: $Q/Q_o=1-\theta^*_o\times$ (shape factor from the book). Remember $Q_o=\rho cV\theta_i$.
Plane wall with both faces exposed uses half-thickness. If only one face is exposed and the other is adiabatic, the full thickness is $L$.
pitfalls: Using $L_c=V/A$ in this $Bi$ — here it is $L$ or $r_o$.
Using the one-term formula when $Fo<0.2$.
Mixing up $\theta^*_o$ (center) with the surface value.
samples: Test 2 guide: §5.4, §5.5 and the first half of Table 5.1

recall.q: When do you use the one-term series, and how are $Bi$ and $Fo$ defined for it?
recall.a: When $Bi>0.1$ (not lumped) and $Fo>0.2$. $Fo=\alpha t/L^2$, $Bi=hL/k$ with $L$ the half-thickness (plane wall) or $r_o$ (cylinder, sphere).

recall.q: Give the sequence for the temperature at a point in a wall.
recall.a: Find $\zeta_1,C_1$ (Table 5.1) from $Bi$; center $\theta_o^*=C_1e^{-\zeta_1^2Fo}$; then the position factor ($\cos\zeta_1x^*$, $J_0$, or $\sin/\zeta_1r^*$). Energy from $Q/Q_o$.

recall.q: A plane wall is insulated on one face and heated on the other. What is $L$?
recall.a: The insulated face is a symmetry plane, so $L$ is the full thickness.

problems.title: Pick the transient model, then the center temperature
problems.statement: A plane wall of thickness $2L=50$ mm ($k=20$ W/m·K, $\alpha=5\times10^{-6}$ m²/s) at $300^\circ$C is suddenly exposed on both faces to fluid at $20^\circ$C with $h=200$ W/m²K. (a) Compute $Bi$ and $Fo$ at $t=60$ s and say which model applies (lumped, one-term, or neither). (b) Find the center temperature.
problems.hint: Both numbers use the half-thickness $L$, not $V/A$.

steps: $Bi=hL/k=0.250>0.1$, so lumped capacitance is not valid. $Fo=\alpha t/L^2=0.480>0.2$, so the one-term series is valid.

problems.title: Heating a slab: one-term solution (plane wall)
problems.statement: A concrete-like slab of thickness $2L=100$ mm ($k=1.2$ W/m·K, $\alpha=6\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$) is initially uniform at $20^\circ$C and is suddenly exposed on both faces to gas at $400^\circ$C with $h=100\ \mathrm{W/m^2K}$. After $t=30$ min find (a) the midplane temperature, (b) the surface temperature, and (c) the energy absorbed per unit area. State whether the one-term approximation is valid. (Solve the eigenvalue equation $\zeta\tan\zeta=Bi$ or interpolate Table 5.1.)
problems.hint: Check $Fo>0.2$ before trusting the one-term form. Surface values use $\cos(\zeta_1x^*)$ at $x^*=1$.

steps: $Bi=hL/k=4.167$ (not lumped — spatial gradients matter). $Fo=\alpha t/L^2=0.432>0.2$ ✓ so one term is accurate.
Energy: $Q/Q_o=1-\dfrac{\sin\zeta_1}{\zeta_1}\theta_0^*=0.5417$ with $Q_o=\rho c(2L)(T_\infty-T_i)=7.60\times10^{7}$ J/m² (using $\rho c=k/\alpha$), so $Q=4.12\times10^{7}$ J/m².

problems.title: Cooling a long steel cylinder
problems.statement: A long steel cylinder of radius $r_o=30$ mm ($k=15$ W/m·K, $\alpha=3.9\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$) leaves a furnace at $600^\circ$C and is cooled in air at $30^\circ$C with $h=250\ \mathrm{W/m^2K}$. After $t=100$ s find the centerline and surface temperatures. Is lumped capacitance acceptable? (One-term series for a cylinder: $\theta^*=C_1e^{-\zeta_1^2Fo}J_0(\zeta_1r^*)$ with $\zeta_1J_1(\zeta_1)/J_0(\zeta_1)=Bi$.)
problems.hint: For a cylinder the characteristic length in the lumped check is $r_o/2$, but the Heisler/one-term $Bi$ uses $r_o$.

steps: $Bi=hr_o/k=0.500$. With $L_c=r_o/2$, $Bi_{lump}=0.250>0.1$, so lumped capacitance is **not** acceptable.
Surface: $\theta^*=\theta_0^*J_0(\zeta_1)=0.6004$, $T_s=372.2^\circ$C (a 91 K gradient across the cylinder).

know: Semi-infinite: valid when the thermal wave has not reached the far side (penetration depth $\approx2\sqrt{\alpha t}$). Three surface cases: constant $T_s$, constant flux, convection.
Constant surface temperature: $T(x,t)$ via $\mathrm{erf}(x/2\sqrt{\alpha t})$ and surface flux $\propto t^{-1/2}$.
Explicit FD: $T_m^{p+1}=Fo(T_{m+1}^p+T_{m-1}^p)+(1-2Fo)T_m^p$; stable only for $Fo\le1/2$. A convective surface node is stricter: $Fo(1+Bi)\le1/2$.
Implicit FD is unconditionally stable but needs a system solve each time step.
pitfalls: Using semi-infinite results after the wave reaches the back surface.
Forgetting to check stability for the convective node.
Using $\Delta t$ that satisfies the interior limit but not the surface limit.
samples: Test 2 guide mentions Ch 5 finite-difference solutions

recall.q: When is the semi-infinite model valid, and how deep does a temperature change reach?
recall.a: Until the thermal wave reaches the far side. Penetration depth is about $2\sqrt{\alpha t}$, which must be much less than the thickness.

recall.q: Write the constant-surface-temperature solution and surface flux.
recall.a: $\dfrac{T-T_s}{T_i-T_s}=\mathrm{erf}\!\left(\dfrac{x}{2\sqrt{\alpha t}}\right)$; $q''_s=k(T_s-T_i)/\sqrt{\pi\alpha t}$, which falls as $t^{-1/2}$.

recall.q: State the stability limits of explicit finite difference.
recall.a: Interior nodes $Fo\le\tfrac12$; a convective surface node is stricter, $Fo(1+Bi)\le\tfrac12$. Use the smaller $\Delta t$.

problems.title: Frost penetration into soil (semi-infinite solid)
problems.statement: Soil initially at $T_i=5^\circ$C (thermal diffusivity $\alpha=0.5\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$) has its surface suddenly held at $T_s=-15^\circ$C for 30 days. Ignoring latent heat, how deep is the $0^\circ$C isotherm? Write the solution you use and the similarity variable.
problems.hint: Penetration depth scales as $\sqrt{\alpha t}$: four times as long, only twice as deep.

steps: Constant surface temperature, semi-infinite solid: $\dfrac{T(x,t)-T_s}{T_i-T_s}=\mathrm{erf}\!\left(\dfrac{x}{2\sqrt{\alpha t}}\right)$.

problems.title: Why tile feels colder than wood (contact temperature)
problems.statement: Treat skin and the floor as semi-infinite solids that are suddenly brought into contact. Skin at $33^\circ$C ($k=0.37$, $\rho=1000$, $c=3500$ in SI units) touches (i) ceramic tile at $18^\circ$C ($k=1.0$, $\rho=2000$, $c=800$) and (ii) wood at $18^\circ$C ($k=0.15$, $\rho=700$, $c=1600$). Find the contact temperature in each case.
problems.hint: Compare the effusivities, not the thermal conductivities alone.

steps: For two semi-infinite solids in perfect contact the interface temperature is constant: $T_s=\dfrac{e_1T_1+e_2T_2}{e_1+e_2}$ with effusivity $e=\sqrt{k\rho c}$.
Tile: $T_s=25.1^\circ$C. Wood: $T_s=29.0^\circ$C. High effusivity pulls the interface toward the floor temperature, so tile feels colder.

problems.method: Contact temperature of two semi-infinite solids

problems.title: Explicit finite-difference: stability and one time step
problems.statement: A solid ($k=2.0$ W/m·K, $\alpha=1\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$) is modeled in 1-D with $\Delta x=10$ mm, with a convective surface ($h=100$ W/m²K, $T_\infty=20^\circ$C). (a) Find the maximum stable time step for the interior nodes and for the surface node. (b) Using $\Delta t=30$ s, advance one step for an interior node (at $70^\circ$C with neighbors $90^\circ$C and $60^\circ$C) and for the surface node (at $75^\circ$C with interior neighbor at $65^\circ$C).
problems.hint: Stability is checked for every node type; the convective surface node is the strictest.

steps: $Bi=h\Delta x/k=0.50$. Interior stability: $Fo\le\tfrac12\Rightarrow\Delta t\le\dfrac{\Delta x^2}{2\alpha}=50$ s. Surface node: $Fo(1+Bi)\le\tfrac12\Rightarrow\Delta t\le33.3$ s. The surface node governs.
$\Delta t=30$ s gives $Fo=0.30$ (stable, since 30 s < <dts:.1f>> s).

know: Velocity, thermal and concentration boundary layers: $\delta$, $\delta_t$, $\delta_c$ and how $Pr$ and $Sc$ set their ratios.
Local $h_x$ vs average $\bar h=\frac1L\int h_xdx$. Flat-plate transition at $Re_{x,c}\approx5\times10^5$.
The four boundary-layer equations: continuity, $x$-momentum, energy, species. They share one form, so one solution gives analogous results for all.
Dimensionless groups: $Nu=hL/k$ (surface gradient), $Pr=\nu/\alpha$, $Re$, $St=Nu/(RePr)$, $Cf$. Physical meaning: Section 6.6.
Analogies: Reynolds and Chilton–Colburn, $St\,Pr^{2/3}=Cf/2$ for $0.6<Pr<60$ and $dp/dx\approx0$.

eq.label: Energy BL
eq.tex: u\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial x}+v\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial y}=\alpha\dfrac{\partial^2T}{\partial y^2}

pitfalls: Evaluating properties at the wrong temperature (use the film temperature unless told otherwise).
Confusing local and average coefficients.
Applying the analogy to flows with large pressure gradients.

recall.q: Write $Re$, $Pr$, $Nu$ and $St$ and say what each compares.
recall.a: $Re=u_\infty x/\nu$ (inertia vs viscous), $Pr=\nu/\alpha$ (momentum vs thermal diffusion), $Nu=hL/k$ (convection vs conduction in the fluid), $St=Nu/RePr=h/\rho u_\infty c_p$.

recall.q: Which boundary layer is thicker, velocity or thermal, for $Pr>1$ and for $Pr<1$?
recall.a: Roughly $\delta_t/\delta\sim Pr^{-1/3}$. For $Pr>1$ (oils, water) the thermal layer is thinner; for $Pr<1$ (liquid metals) it is thicker; gases are about equal.

recall.q: State the Chilton–Colburn analogy and when it applies.
recall.a: $St\,Pr^{2/3}=Cf/2$, for $0.6<Pr<60$ and negligible pressure gradient ($dp/dx\approx0$).

problems.title: Dimensionless groups from a measurement
problems.statement: Water flows at $u_\infty=2.0$ m/s over a plate of length $L=0.20$ m and the measured average coefficient is $\bar h=3000$ W/m²K. Use water at 300 K: $k=0.613$ W/m·K, $\nu=0.855\times10^{-6}$ m²/s, $\mu=855\times10^{-6}$ kg/m·s, $Pr=5.83$. Compute $Re_L$, $\overline{Nu}_L$ and the Stanton number, and say whether the thermal boundary layer is thicker or thinner than the velocity boundary layer.
problems.hint: $St=Nu/(Re\,Pr)=h/(\rho u_\infty c_p)$.

steps: Because $Pr=5.83>1$, momentum diffuses faster than heat, so $\delta_t<\delta$ ($\delta_t/\delta\sim Pr^{-1/3}$).

problems.title: Laminar boundary layer on a flat plate
problems.statement: Air at 300 K ($k=0.0263$ W/m·K, $\nu=15.89\times10^{-6}$ m²/s, $Pr=0.707$, $\rho=1.161$ kg/m³) flows at $U_\infty=5$ m/s over a flat plate of length $L=1$ m. (a) Is the flow laminar over the whole plate? (b) At $x=0.4$ m find the hydrodynamic and thermal boundary-layer thicknesses, the local friction coefficient and wall shear stress, and the local convection coefficient. (c) Find the average coefficient over $0<x<L$. Use $\delta=5x/\sqrt{Re_x}$, $\delta_t=\delta Pr^{-1/3}$, $Cf_x=0.664Re_x^{-1/2}$, $Nu_x=0.332Re_x^{1/2}Pr^{1/3}$.

know: $Re_D=4\dot m/\pi D\mu$; laminar below about 2300. Entry lengths: laminar $x_{fd,h}\approx0.05Re_DD$, $x_{fd,t}\approx0.05Re_DPrD$; turbulent about $10D$.

Laminar, fully developed: $Nu_D=4.36$ (const. flux), $3.66$ (const. $T_s$). Non-circular tubes use the hydraulic diameter $D_h=4A_c/P$.
Turbulent: Dittus–Boelter ($n=0.4$ heating, $0.3$ cooling), or Gnielinski for more accuracy.
Overall problem: find $Re$ → pick correlation → $\bar h$ → use $NTU$-type exponential or $\Delta T_{lm}$ for outlet temperature.

eq.label: Const. $T_s$
eq.tex: \dfrac{T_s-T_{m,o}}{T_s-T_{m,i}}=\exp\!\left(-\dfrac{\pi DL\,\bar h}{\dot m c_p}\right),\ \ q=\bar hA_s\Delta T_{lm}

pitfalls: Averaging inlet and outlet temperatures instead of using the exponential/log-mean.
Using the wrong $n$ for heating vs cooling.
Using laminar $Nu$ in the entry region.

recall.q: Write $Re_D$ and the laminar threshold. What are the entry lengths?
recall.a: $Re_D=4\dot m/\pi D\mu$; laminar below about 2300. Hydrodynamic entry $0.05Re_DD$, thermal $0.05Re_DPrD$, turbulent about $10D$.

recall.q: Give the fully developed laminar $Nu_D$ values and the hydraulic diameter.
recall.a: 4.36 for constant flux, 3.66 for constant $T_s$ (circular tube). $D_h=4A_c/P$ for other shapes.

recall.q: How does $T_m$ change along the tube for constant $q''_s$ versus constant $T_s$? Which Dittus–Boelter exponent for heating and cooling?
recall.a: Constant flux: $T_m$ rises linearly. Constant $T_s$: $T_s-T_m$ decays exponentially (use $\Delta T_{lm}$). $n=0.4$ heating, $0.3$ cooling.

know: $q=UA\Delta T_{lm}$ with $\Delta T_{lm}$ for counterflow ($\Delta T_1=T_{h,i}-T_{c,o}$) or parallel flow ($\Delta T_1=T_{h,i}-T_{c,i}$). Use correction factor $F$ for cross-flow and multipass.
Overall coefficient $1/UA=R_{h}+R_{f}+R_{wall}+R_{c}$ — resistances add, same as Chapter 3.
$\varepsilon=q/q_{max}$, $q_{max}=C_{min}(T_{h,i}-T_{c,i})$, $NTU=UA/C_{min}$, $C_r=C_{min}/C_{max}$. Tables 11.3–11.4 give $\varepsilon$ ↔ NTU for each flow arrangement.
Boiling/condensing ($C_r=0$): $\varepsilon=1-e^{-NTU}$ for every configuration.
Counterflow is always at least as effective as parallel flow for the same $UA$.

eq.label: Heat rate
eq.tex: q=UA\,\Delta T_{lm},\quad \Delta T_{lm}=\dfrac{\Delta T_1-\Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1/\Delta T_2)}

pitfalls: Mislabeling $\Delta T_1$ and $\Delta T_2$ for counterflow.
Using the cold-stream capacity rate as $C_{min}$ without checking.
Applying LMTD when outlet temperatures are unknown — use NTU.
samples: No Ch 11 slides or homework are posted on Canvas — rely on the book and these videos

recall.q: When do you use LMTD and when ε–NTU?
recall.a: LMTD when all four terminal temperatures are known (design). ε–NTU when outlets are unknown (rating).

recall.q: Define $C$, $C_{min}$, $C_r$, NTU and $\varepsilon$.
recall.a: $C=\dot mc_p$; $C_r=C_{min}/C_{max}$; $NTU=UA/C_{min}$; $\varepsilon=q/q_{max}$ with $q_{max}=C_{min}(T_{h,i}-T_{c,i})$.

recall.q: What happens when $C_r=0$ (boiling or condensing), and which flow arrangement is best?
recall.a: $\varepsilon=1-e^{-NTU}$ for every arrangement. Counterflow is at least as effective as parallel flow for the same $UA$.

know: Buoyancy drives the flow. $Gr_L=g\beta\Delta TL^3/\nu^2$, $Ra_L=Gr_LPr$; $\beta=1/T_f$ for ideal gases (kelvin!).
Vertical plate transition at $Ra_L\approx10^9$. Churchill–Chu full-range correlation works for all $Ra$; the laminar-only form needs $Ra\le10^9$.
Horizontal plates: hot side up (or cold side down) $Nu=0.54Ra^{1/4}$ or $0.15Ra^{1/3}$; hot side down $Nu=0.52Ra^{1/5}$ (check Table 9.3). Characteristic length $L=A_s/P$.
Horizontal cylinder and sphere: Churchill–Chu forms; enclosures use cavity correlations (§9.8).
Mixed convection when $Gr/Re^2\approx1$: combine $Nu^n=Nu_F^n\pm Nu_N^n$ ($n=3$ for most cases).
Natural convection $h$ is small, so radiation is often comparable — add $h_r$.
pitfalls: Using °C for $\beta$.
Not computing $Ra$ before choosing.
Forgetting to add radiation.

recall.q: Write the Rayleigh number and the temperature to use in $\beta$.
recall.a: $Ra_L=g\beta(T_s-T_\infty)L^3/\nu\alpha$. For an ideal gas $\beta=1/T_f$ with $T_f$ in kelvin.

recall.q: Where does a vertical plate transition, and which correlations apply?
recall.a: Near $Ra_L\approx10^9$. The Churchill–Chu full-range form works everywhere; the laminar-only form needs $Ra_L\le10^9$.

recall.q: What is the characteristic length for a horizontal plate, and why add $h_r$?
recall.a: $L=A_s/P$. Natural-convection $h$ is small, so radiation is often comparable and must be added.

problems.title: Rayleigh number and flow regime
problems.statement: A vertical plate $L=0.40$ m tall at $350$ K stands in still air at $300$ K. Use air properties at the film temperature: $\nu=18.4\times10^{-6}$ m²/s, $\alpha=26.2\times10^{-6}$ m²/s, $k=0.0282$ W/m·K, $Pr=0.703$. Compute $Ra_L$ (treating air as an ideal gas), decide laminar or turbulent, and find $\bar h$ with the laminar Churchill–Chu form. What error would using °C in $\beta$ cause?
problems.hint: $\beta=1/T_f$ requires kelvin.

steps: $T_f=325$ K, $\beta=1/T_f=3.08\times10^{-3}$ K$^{-1}$. $Ra_L=\dfrac{g\beta\Delta TL^3}{\nu\alpha}=2.00\times10^{8}$, below $10^9$, so the boundary layer is laminar.
Using °C would give $\beta=1/52=0.0193$, overstating $Ra_L$ by a factor of 6.3.

problems.title: Vertical heated plate in still air
problems.statement: A vertical plate $0.6$ m tall and $0.8$ m wide is at $370$ K in quiescent air at $280$ K. Film properties (325 K): $k=0.02815$ W/m·K, $\nu=18.4\times10^{-6}$ m²/s, $\alpha=26.2\times10^{-6}$ m²/s, $Pr=0.7035$, $\beta=1/T_f$. Find $Ra_L$, decide the regime, and compute $\bar h$ and the convective heat rate using the Churchill–Chu full-range correlation $\overline{Nu}_L=\left\{0.825+\dfrac{0.387Ra_L^{1/6}}{[1+(0.492/Pr)^{9/16}]^{8/27}}\right\}^2$.
problems.hint: $\beta=1/T_f$ for an ideal gas, with $T_f$ in kelvin. Compute $Ra$ first to choose the correlation.

steps: $Ra_L=\dfrac{g\beta\Delta TL^3}{\nu\alpha}=1.22\times10^{9}$. Transition for a vertical plate is near $10^9$, so this is turbulent.
Churchill–Chu: $\overline{Nu}_L=130.4$ (the laminar-only form would give 96.6, which is not valid here).

problems.title: Hot pipe in a room: free convection plus radiation
problems.statement: A horizontal pipe of diameter $D=50$ mm at 370 K sits in still air at 280 K (same film properties as 16a); the pipe surface emissivity is $\varepsilon=0.9$ and the room surfaces are at 280 K. Find $Ra_D$, $\bar h$ from the Churchill–Chu horizontal-cylinder correlation $\overline{Nu}_D=\left\{0.6+\dfrac{0.387Ra_D^{1/6}}{[1+(0.559/Pr)^{9/16}]^{8/27}}\right\}^2$, and the convective, radiative and total heat loss per meter.
problems.hint: In natural convection in air, $h$ and $h_r$ are often the same order of magnitude. Add both.

steps: $h_r=\varepsilon\sigma(T_s+T_{sur})(T_s^2+T_{sur}^2)=7.14$ W/m²K — almost the same as $\bar h$, so radiation carries about half of the total loss.
$q'_{conv}=\bar h\pi D\Delta T=104.8$ W/m; $q'_{rad}=h_r\pi D\Delta T=101.0$ W/m; total $=205.7$ W/m.

know: Blackbody: $E_b=\sigma T^4$; spectral shape from Planck; Wien: $\lambda_{max}T=2898\ \mu$m·K.
Band emission via $F_{(0\to\lambda T)}$ from Table 12.2: $E_{\lambda_1\to\lambda_2}=[F(\lambda_2T)-F(\lambda_1T)]E_b$.
Real surfaces: $E=\varepsilon E_b$. Irradiation splits: $\alpha+\rho+\tau=1$ (opaque: $\alpha+\rho=1$).
Kirchhoff: $\varepsilon_\lambda=\alpha_\lambda$ for diffuse surfaces; total $\varepsilon=\alpha$ only if gray or if the irradiation matches the surface temperature.
$\alpha$ depends on the source spectrum (use band fractions at the source temperature); $\varepsilon$ on the surface spectrum.
Intensity: diffuse emission $E=\pi I_e$; solid-angle integrals give irradiation and emissive power.
pitfalls: Using $\varepsilon$ where $\alpha_S$ is needed (and vice versa).
Using Celsius.
Applying Kirchhoff to non-diffuse surfaces or without checking the spectra.

recall.q: Write the blackbody emissive power and Wien's law.
recall.a: $E_b=\sigma T^4$ and $\lambda_{max}T=2898\ \mu$m·K.

recall.q: Give the recipe for the emission in a wavelength band.
recall.a: Look up $F_{(0\to\lambda T)}$ at each end (Table 12.2): $E_{\lambda_1\to\lambda_2}=[F(\lambda_2T)-F(\lambda_1T)]\sigma T^4$.

recall.q: State the energy split of irradiation and when $\varepsilon=\alpha$.
recall.a: $\alpha+\rho+\tau=1$ (opaque: $\alpha+\rho=1$). Kirchhoff $\varepsilon_\lambda=\alpha_\lambda$ for diffuse surfaces; total $\varepsilon=\alpha$ only if gray or if the source temperature matches the surface. $\alpha$ depends on the source spectrum, $\varepsilon$ on the surface spectrum.

problems.title: Irradiation, absorption and radiosity
problems.statement: An opaque, diffuse, gray surface at $500$ K has emissivity $\varepsilon=0.6$ and receives irradiation $G=800\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$. Find the absorbed and reflected irradiation, the emissive power, the radiosity and the net radiative flux leaving the surface.
problems.hint: Radiosity is everything leaving: emitted plus reflected.

steps: Gray and diffuse means $\alpha=\varepsilon=0.6$; opaque means $\rho=1-\alpha=0.4$.
Absorbed $\alpha G=480$ W/m²; reflected $\rho G=320$ W/m². $E=\varepsilon\sigma T^4=2126.2$ W/m².
Radiosity $J=E+\rho G=2446.2$ W/m². Net flux leaving the surface $q''=J-G=E-\alpha G=1646.2$ W/m².

problems.title: Blackbody band emission and Wien's law
problems.statement: A surface at 1000 K emits as a blackbody. Find (a) its total emissive power, (b) the wavelength of peak emission, (c) the fraction and the power of emission between $\lambda_1=2\ \mu$m and $\lambda_2=5\ \mu$m (use the blackbody fraction $F_{(0\to\lambda)}$ vs. $\lambda T$, Table 12.2), (d) the emissive power if the surface were gray with $\varepsilon=0.6$.
problems.hint: Convert wavelengths to $\lambda T$ in $\mu$m·K before using the table.

steps: Gray: $E=\varepsilon\sigma T^4=34020$ W/m² (the same spectral shape, scaled by 0.6).

problems.title: Selective surface in sunlight (Kirchhoff + band properties)
problems.statement: An opaque, diffuse plate facing the sun has $\alpha_\lambda=0.9$ for $\lambda<2\ \mu$m and $\alpha_\lambda=0.2$ for $\lambda>2\ \mu$m. Solar irradiation is $G_S=1000$ W/m² with spectral distribution of a 5800 K blackbody. The back is insulated and the plate radiates to cold space (no convection). (a) Find the solar absorptivity $\alpha_S$. (b) Using Kirchhoff's law ($\varepsilon_\lambda=\alpha_\lambda$ for a diffuse surface), find the total emissivity at the equilibrium temperature and the equilibrium temperature itself.
problems.hint: $\alpha$ is averaged with the **source** spectrum, $\varepsilon$ with the **surface** spectrum (set by its own temperature).

steps: Absorptivity is a solar-weighted average: $\lambda T_{sun}=2\times5800=11{,}600\ \mu$m·K gives $F_{(0\to2\mu m)}=0.9402$. $\alpha_S=0.9F+0.2(1-F)=0.8581$.

Equilibrium: $\alpha_SG_S=\varepsilon(T)\sigma T^4$ with $\varepsilon(T)=0.9F_{(0\to2T)}+0.2[1-F_{(0\to2T)}]$. At the plate temperature $\lambda T=2T\approx1048\ \mu$m·K is tiny, so $F\approx0$ and $\varepsilon\approx0.2004$.
Iterating: $T_{eq}=524$ K ($\approx251^\circ$C). A black surface would reach only $(G_S/\sigma)^{1/4}=364$ K; the selective coating runs much hotter.

know: View factor $F_{ij}$: fraction of radiation leaving $i$ that reaches $j$. Rules: reciprocity $A_iF_{ij}=A_jF_{ji}$, summation $\sum_jF_{ij}=1$, superposition, symmetry. Table 13.1–13.2 give common geometries.
Black surfaces: $q_{ij}=A_iF_{ij}\sigma(T_i^4-T_j^4)$.
Gray diffuse enclosure: surface resistance $(1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon A$ and space resistance $1/A_iF_{ij}$ in a network between $E_b$ and radiosity $J$ nodes.
Special cases (Table 13.3): large parallel plates, long concentric cylinders/spheres, small object in a large cavity.
Radiation shields add two surface resistances and one space resistance per gap; they reduce the exchange by roughly $1/(N+1)$ for equal emissivities.
pitfalls: Forgetting that a flat or convex surface has $F_{ii}=0$.
Using $\varepsilon$ where radiosity is needed.
Dropping a surface resistance for a low-emissivity surface (it often dominates).
samples: No Ch 13 slides or homework are posted on Canvas — rely on the book and these videos

recall.q: State the view-factor rules and the self-view factor of a flat or convex surface.
recall.a: Reciprocity $A_iF_{ij}=A_jF_{ji}$; summation $\sum_jF_{ij}=1$; superposition and symmetry. $F_{ii}=0$ for flat or convex surfaces.

recall.q: Name the two kinds of resistance in a gray diffuse enclosure and write them.
recall.a: Surface $(1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon A$ (between $E_b$ and $J$) and space $1/A_iF_{ij}$ (between radiosities).

recall.q: Write the net flux between large parallel plates and the effect of $N$ shields.
recall.a: $q''_{12}=\sigma(T_1^4-T_2^4)/(1/\varepsilon_1+1/\varepsilon_2-1)$. With $N$ shields of equal emissivity the exchange drops to about $1/(N+1)$.

problems.title: Concentric spheres: reciprocity and summation
problems.statement: A black sphere of diameter $D_1=0.20$ m sits inside a larger black spherical shell of diameter $D_2=0.50$ m. Find $F_{11}$, $F_{12}$, $F_{21}$ and $F_{22}$. If the inner sphere is at $600$ K and the shell at $300$ K, find the net radiation from the inner sphere.
problems.hint: Flat or convex surfaces cannot see themselves: $F_{ii}=0$.

steps: The inner sphere is convex and fully enclosed: $F_{11}=0$ and, by summation, $F_{12}=1$.

problems.title: View factors in a long triangular duct
problems.statement: A long duct has a right-triangle cross-section with sides $w_1=0.3$ m, $w_2=0.4$ m and $w_3=0.5$ m (flat surfaces, no self-view). (a) Find all nine view factors using the summation rule, reciprocity and (for a triangle) the crossed-strings form $F_{12}=(w_1+w_2-w_3)/(2w_1)$. (b) If surfaces 1 and 2 are black at 500 K and 300 K, find the net radiation from 1 to 2 per unit length.
problems.hint: Use reciprocity to get the 'backwards' factors, summation to finish each row.

problems.title: Radiation shield between large parallel plates
problems.statement: Two large parallel gray plates have $T_1=600$ K, $\varepsilon_1=0.7$ and $T_2=300$ K, $\varepsilon_2=0.5$. (a) Find the net radiation flux between them. (b) A thin shield with $\varepsilon_3=0.1$ on both sides is placed midway. Find the new flux and the shield temperature. By what percentage does the shield cut the exchange?
problems.hint: Treat each gap as a two-plate exchange and add the resistances in series.

steps: With shield, two gaps in series: $R_{13}=1/\varepsilon_1+1/\varepsilon_3-1=10.43$, $R_{32}=1/\varepsilon_3+1/\varepsilon_2-1=11.00$, so $q''=\dfrac{\sigma(T_1^4-T_2^4)}{R_{13}+R_{32}}=321$ W/m².
Shield temperature from the first gap: $\sigma(T_1^4-T_3^4)=q''R_{13}\Rightarrow T_3=515$ K.
Reduction: $1-q''_{shield}/q''_{12}=89$% — a low-emissivity shield is very effective.

contrasts.pair: Lumped capacitance vs one-term series vs semi-infinite solid
contrasts.decide: Compute $Bi=hL_c/k$ first: $Bi<0.1$ is lumped. If $Bi>0.1$ and $Fo>0.2$ use the one-term series. If the thermal wave has not reached the far side ($2\sqrt{\alpha t}\ll$ thickness) use the semi-infinite solid.

contrasts.pair: Series thermal circuit vs shape factor
contrasts.decide: One-dimensional layers between fluids: resistance circuit. Two isothermal surfaces with 2-D geometry (buried pipe, sphere): $q=Sk\Delta T$.

contrasts.pair: Fin with adiabatic tip vs convective tip
contrasts.decide: Use $q_f=M\tanh mL$. If the tip loses heat, replace $L$ by the corrected length $L_c=L+A_c/P$; do not use the infinite-fin result for a short fin.
Compare $x_c=Re_{x,c}\nu/u_\infty$ with $L$ (or $Re_L$ with $5\times10^5$). If transition falls inside the plate, use the mixed average correlation.
Free stream over a body: film temperature, $Re_L$ or $Re_D$ with threshold $5\times10^5$. Confined in a tube: mean temperature $T_m$, $Re_D=4\dot m/\pi D\mu$ with threshold 2300.

contrasts.pair: Constant wall temperature vs constant heat flux in a tube
contrasts.decide: Constant $T_s$: $T_s-T_m$ decays exponentially, use $\Delta T_{lm}$, laminar $Nu=3.66$. Constant $q''_s$: $T_m$ is linear in $x$, $T_s-T_m=q''_s/h$, laminar $Nu=4.36$.

contrasts.pair: Forced vs natural vs mixed convection
contrasts.decide: Compare $Gr/Re^2$: much less than 1 is forced, much greater is natural, about 1 is mixed ($Nu^3=Nu_F^3\pm Nu_N^3$).

contrasts.pair: Churchill–Bernstein vs Hilpert for a cylinder
contrasts.decide: Churchill–Bernstein is one formula for $Re_DPr>0.2$. Hilpert needs $C$ and $m$ from the $Re_D$ band in Table 7.2.
All four terminal temperatures known: LMTD (design, find $A$). Outlets unknown: ε–NTU (rating). Boiling or condensing ($C_r=0$): $\varepsilon=1-e^{-NTU}$.

contrasts.pair: Film temperature vs mean temperature for properties
contrasts.decide: External flow and free convection: film temperature $(T_s+T_\infty)/2$. Internal flow: mean temperature $T_m$ (average of inlet and outlet).
$\varepsilon$ comes from the surface's own spectrum (surface temperature); $\alpha_S$ from the Sun's spectrum (about 5800 K). A selective surface can have very different values.
Explicit is easy but needs $Fo\le\tfrac12$ (and $Fo(1+Bi)\le\tfrac12$ at a convective surface). Implicit is unconditionally stable but needs a system solve each step.

contrasts.pair: Black-surface exchange vs gray diffuse enclosure
contrasts.decide: Black: $q=A_iF_{ij}\sigma(T_i^4-T_j^4)$. Gray: add a surface resistance $(1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon A$ at every surface and use radiosity nodes.
